tagline: Longleaf pine and wet savannahs line a forest drive toward Sumatra.
intro: The Apalachee Savannahs Scenic Byway crosses flat to gently rolling ground in the western Apalachicola National Forest. Longleaf pines stand scattered across grassland, with cypress swamps, magnolia bays and oak hammocks along the way. The Forest Service emphasizes the route’s plant life, including orchids, pitcher plants and sundews; the Federal Highway Administration suggests allowing an hour and a half. The savannahs often hold water throughout the year, while longleaf pine also grows in the sandhills and flatwoods.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt established the national forest by proclamation in 1936. Its open pine communities depend on frequent fire, which maintains the grassland conditions favored by red-cockaded woodpeckers. Near the byway’s southern end, Prospect Bluff preserves the ruins of two forts: a British fort built in 1814 and Fort Gadsden, built within its former walls in 1818. U.S. forces destroyed the earlier fort in 1816, after it had become a community of people escaping slavery.

The Forest Service itinerary begins on SR 12 at the forest boundary nine miles south of Bristol. It follows SR 12 for almost four miles, turns onto SR 379, passes through Sumatra and takes SR 65 south to the forest’s southern tip. The same page lists 32 miles and a temporary closure due to tropical weather.

moments.title: Longleaf pine savannahs
moments.text: The forest along this byway includes open ground: grasslands dotted with longleaf pine, with wiregrass or palmetto beneath the trees. The savannahs often hold water throughout the year, and their plants include pitcher plants, sundews and wild orchids. Frequent surface fires maintain the open longleaf-pine grassland used by red-cockaded woodpeckers. Along the drive, that pine country is interspersed with swamps and savannahs, while the Forest Service also identifies oak hammocks and magnolia bays. The national forest’s pine flatwoods occupy broad, sandy flatlands; its sandhills are woodlands dominated by longleaf pine.
moments.notice: Scattered longleaf pines rise above wiregrass or palmetto.

moments.title: Sumatra
moments.text: Sumatra is the byway’s community on State Road 65, within Liberty County. The highway and the Apalachicola Northern Railroad run parallel south of town, crossing the Franklin-Liberty county line together. The Forest Service itinerary turns south along SR 65 here; Prospect Bluff lies six miles southwest of Sumatra on the Apalachicola River.

moments.title: Prospect Bluff Historic Sites
moments.text: Two forts occupied this bluff above the Apalachicola River, but their histories are distinct. The British built the first in 1814. After their withdrawal in 1815, members of the disbanded Corps of Colonial Marines, largely people who had escaped slavery, and Creek tribesmen occupied it. It became a growing community of people escaping slavery before U.S. forces destroyed the fort in 1816. Fort Gadsden followed in 1818, built inside the earlier earthworks. The later fort was abandoned in 1821, when Florida became a U.S. territory and there was no longer a national border to defend. The site contains ruins of both forts and interpretive signs.

practical: Longleaf pine savannahs: The Forest Service page, updated October 9, 2026, lists the byway site as temporarily closed due to tropical weather. (checked 2026-10-11)
